19228.t: BM3244: Translational Technologies for Medical Industry
19228.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM3244 : Translational Technologies for Medical Industry { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Fundamentals of Translational Medicine and Medical Technology Development
• Concept of translational medicine and its importance in healthcare
• Bench-to-bedside approach: bridging laboratory research and clinical application
• Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs) and product development lifecycle
• Regulatory pathways for medical devices and biomaterials (FDA, CDSCO)
• Case studies of successful translational medical technologies
Module 2: Advanced Biomedical Technologies
• Biomaterials for implants and tissue engineering
• Biosensors and lab-on-a-chip diagnostics
• Drug delivery innovations: nanoparticles, smart hydrogels, and controlled release systems
• Medical robotics and AI-driven healthcare technologies
• 3D bioprinting and organ-on-a-chip systems for regenerative medicine
Module 3: Biomedical Device Prototyping and Manufacturing
• Rapid prototyping and 3D printing in medical technology
• MEMS and microfabrication for diagnostics and drug delivery
• Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) and quality control in biomedical industries
• Pilot-scale production and scalability challenges
• Industry collaborations and technology transfer strategies
Module 4: Industrial Developments and Regulatory Requirements
• Medical device industry landscape and market trends
• Product development challenges: clinical validation and reimbursement policies
• Intellectual property (IP), patents, and technology licensing
• Entrepreneurship and funding opportunities for biomedical startups
• Case studies of industry-driven biomedical innovations
Module 5: Future Trends and Emerging Technologies
• AI and big data in predictive healthcare and personalized medicine
• Smart biomaterials and bioelectronics for next-gen therapies
• Theranostics: integrated diagnostics and therapeutics
• Ethical, societal, and economic aspects of medical technology translation

Course Objective

1 .

To introduce students to the principles of translational medicine and the process of developing medical technologies from research to clinical application.
2 .

To familiarize students with advanced biomedical technologies, including biomaterials, biosensors, drug delivery systems, and medical robotics.
3 .

To provide an understanding of prototyping, manufacturing, and regulatory requirements for biomedical devices and diagnostics.
4 .

To equip students with knowledge of industrial developments, commercialization strategies, and future trends in medical technology innovation.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Students will be able to explain the translational process and regulatory pathways for bringing biomedical technologies to market.
2. Students will demonstrate an understanding of cutting-edge biomedical technologies and their clinical applications.
3. Students will gain practical insights into biomedical device prototyping, manufacturing standards, and industry best practices.
4. Students will be able to analyze industrial requirements, intellectual property considerations, and commercialization strategies for medical innovations.
5. Students will develop critical thinking skills to assess future trends and challenges in translational biomedical engineering.

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM4344 : Bioinstrumentation in Environment Management { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Introduction to Bioinstrumentation & Environmental Monitoring
Basics of bioinstrumentation, types of instruments, and their role in monitoring environmental parameters like air and water quality. Methods for collecting and preparing air, water, and soil samples for analysis.
Module 2: Environment Monitoring Instruments
Air Quality: Tools like gas chromatography, infrared spectroscopy, and mass spectrometry to detect pollutants in the air. Water Quality: Instruments like pH sensors, dissolved oxygen meters, and ion chromatography for measuring water pollutants. Soil & Sediment Analysis: Techniques for testing soil composition, contamination, and microbial activity using bioinstrumentation.
Module 3: Biotechnology in Environmental Management
Bioremediation, bioassays, and biosensors to address environmental pollution and contamination.
Module 4: Data Analysis & Interpretation
Methods for collecting, analyzing, and interpreting environmental data using statistical tools.
Module 5: Regulatory Standards & Policies
Overview of international environmental standards, pollution control policies, and the role of bioinstrumentation in compliance and assessment.
Module 6: Emerging Trends in Bioinstrumentation
Exploration of new technologies like nanotechnology, IoT, and smart sensors in environmental monitoring.

Course Objective

1 .

1. To provide students with a thorough understanding of bioinstrumentation tools and techniques used in environmental monitoring, focusing on their principles, operation, and application to environmental management.
2 .

2. To teach students how to interpret and analyze data collected from bioinstrumental tools, applying statistical methods to derive meaningful insights for environmental decision-making
3 .

3. To familiarize students with international and national environmental regulations and the role of bioinstrumentation in ensuring compliance with pollution control standards and environmental impact assessments.
4 .

4. To encourage the development of innovative approaches to solving real-world environmental challenges using bioinstrumentation and emerging technologies like smart sensors and IoT.

Course Outcome

1 .

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
1. Articulate the significance of bioinstrumentation in monitoring environmental systems and managing natural resources like air, water, and soil.
2. Demonstrate proficiency in using various environmental bioinstrumentation tools, such as gas chromatographs, spectrometers, sensors, and biosensors, for collecting and analyzing environmental data.
3. Understand and apply relevant environmental regulations and standards (e.g., ISO, EPA) in the context of bioinstrumentation-based environmental monitoring and compliance.
4. Utilize bioinstrumentation techniques to identify pollution sources and suggest effective pollution control measures, including the use of bioremediation and sustainable practices.
5. Stay informed about advancements in bioinstrumentation, such as nanotechnology, smart sensors, and IoT, and their potential to transform environmental monitoring and management.

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CE6133 : Earthquake Geotechnical Engineering { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Causes and characteristics (magnitude, intensity, accelarograms), response spectra, attenuation of ground motion. Estimation of seismic hazards (deterministic and probabilistic). [10 hrs]
Module 2: Introduction to vibratory motion: Waves in Elastic Medium, Dynamics of Discrete Systems, Vibration of single and multiple degree of freedom systems. Free and forced vibrations (regular and irregular excitation) [8 hrs]
Module 3: Dynamic properties of soils: Determination of site characteristics, local geology and soil condition, site investigation and soil test, Laboratory and in-situ tests, Site response to earthquake, Seismic Microzonation. [10 hrs]
Module 4: Liquefaction of soils: Fundamental concept of liquefaction, assessment of liquefaction susceptibility from SPT and CPT, Seismic response of soil structure system, seismic bearing capacity of shallow foundation, design of pile foundation in liquefiable ground. Pseudo-static analysis and design of earth retaining structures and soil slopes, Estimation of earthquake-induced deformation. [12 hrs]

Course Objective

1 .

Able to understand the causes of earthquake and know it's associated parameters
2 .

Able to know how to determine the dynamic soil properties
3 .

Able to carry out liquefaction susceptibility analysis
4 .

Design of some geotechnical structures subjected to earthquake

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Learn about the causes of earthquake, response spectra and attenuation relationship for ground motion parameters.
2. Understand vibratory motions, seismic waves and various field tests as well as laboratory tests conducted to determine dynamic soil properties
3. Apply the principles of seismic hazard analysis to develop a seismic zonation map of a particular city or region.
4. Evaluate liquefaction susceptibility analysis of a particular site
5. Design/Analysis of geotechnical structures subjected to earthquake/vibration

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : EC6506 : Information Theory and Coding { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

MODULE-I: Discrete Information Sources: Source alphabets and entropy. Joint and conditional entropy, Entropy, Entropy of symbol blocks and chain rule, Relative and Mutual information. Joint information. Conditional information, Jensen’s Inequality, Log-Sum Inequality, Fano’s Inequality. [04 Hours]
MODULE-II: Asymptotic Equipartition property, Markov Chain, Entropy Rates, Markov source, and source with memory. Markov chain, Entropy rates. [04 Hours]
MODULE-III: Source coding. Kraft Inequality, Source Coding Theorem, Prefix Codes, Optimal Codes, Huffman coding, Shanon Fano Coding, dictionary codes and Lempel-Ziv Coding. Arithmetic coding. [05 Hours]
MODULE-IV: Information Channels, Mutual information of channels, Channel Capacity, Examples of Channel Capacity, Reliable Messages and Unreliable Channels, Example of Coding to correct errors, Shannon’s Second theorem. [08 Hours]
MODULE-IV: Discrete Algebra, Vector Spaces, Convolution codes: Structural properties of convolution codes, Viterbi algorithm for hard decision and soft decision. Puncture Convolution codes. Trellis Coded Modulation: Multi-amplitude/Multi phase discrete memory less channels. Systematic recursive convolution encoder, signal mapping and set partitioning, Trellis codes for PSK and QAM. [15 Hours]

Course Objective

1 .

To build concepts on secure communication by knowing techniques of source coding, channel capacity and channel coding.
2 .

Build in-depth concept on information theoretic approach in coding for digital communication and data compression.
3 .

Masters students will be able to know the operational principle of various encoding and decoding methodologies and their present day advancements and industry requirements.

Course Outcome

1 .

CO1: Develop a basic understanding of the statistical approaches and mathematical tools needed for understanding the information-theoretic perspective of communication.
CO2: Understand how to apply information theory to code the data to be communicated.
CO3: Apply the statistical approaches and tools and develop codes for transmitted data .
CO4: Develop an indepth understanding of how to transmit information securely through unreliable channels by applying the concept of information theory to channels.
CO5: Extend the knowledge gained in information theory to design various error control codes and their respective encoding and decoding schemes Apply the knowledge to design new error control coding schemes.

Essential Reading

1 .

Thomas M. Cover, Joy A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory,, Wiley , 2nd Edition 2006

2 .

Shu Lin and Daniel Jr. Costello,, Error Control Coding,, Prentice Hall , Second Edition

Supplementary Reading

1 .

Norman Abramson,, Information Theory and Coding,, McGraw Hill , Electronic Sciences Series

2 .

R Bose, Information Theory, Coding and Cryptography, McGraw Hill Education India Private Limited , 2nd Edition 2017

Subject {L-T-P / C} : EC4303 : Biomedical Instrumentation { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: INTRODUCTION:
Generalized Medical Instrumentation System, Roles of Engineering in Healthcare systems, Biometrics, Problems encountered in measuring physiological parameters. (6 hrs.)
Module 2: PHYSIOLOGICAL TRANSDUCERS:
Various types of transducers for measurement of temperature, pressure, flow etc. and their selection for medical applications, Different types of electrodes. (6 hrs.)
Module 3: ELECTRIC SIGNALS AND ELECTRONICS:
Origin of bio-electric signals, Bioelectric potentials, Biopotential electrodes, Measurement of electrical activities in heart, muscles and brain: Electrocardiograph, Electroencephalograph, Electromyograph and their interpretations. (8 hrs.)
Module 4: CARDIOVASCULAR MEASUREMENT:
Electrocardiograph, Measurement of ECG, ECG electrodes, ECG Amplifiers, Common mode interference reduction circuits, Cardiac pacemaker, Phonocardiograph, Measurement of heart rate, Plethysmography. (10 hrs.)
Module 5: DIFFERENT PHYSIOLOGICAL PARAMETERS MEASUREMENT AND MONITORING SYSTEM:
Blood pressure measurement, BLOOD FLOW METERS: Electromagnetic blood flow meter, Ultrasonic blood flow meter, Doppler flow meter, Measurement of temperature, Respiratory System Measurement: Respiration rate measurement, Lung Volume and Capacity, Spirometer, Ventilators, Instrumentation for Clinical laboratory: BLOOD GAS ANALYZERS: Blood pH Measurement, Pulse oximeter, BLOOD CELL COUNTERS: Coulter counters, Automatic recognition and differential counting of cells, GSR measurement Medical Imaging: Ultrasonography, X-ray. (10 hrs.)

Course Objective

1 .

To understand the necessity of Electronics Engineering in health care system and to comprehend different physiological transduction mechanisms to develop the medical equipments.
2 .

To understand the origin and characteristics of different bio-potential signals.
3 .

To grasp knowledge on different physiological parameters measurement systems.
4 .

To grasp knowledge on different monitoring / imaging systems used for health care domain.

Course Outcome

1 .

After the completion of this course, students will be able to:
CO1: explain the transduction mechanism and the basic architecture or the block-diagram of instrumentation system used for biomedical signal acquisition.
CO2: describe the different basic physiological activities and their characteristics, such as generation of the different bio-potential signals, blood flow in human body, activities of heart, blood pressure, etc.
CO3: understand the design principle of capturing different electrical and non-electrical physiological parameters and medical imaging techniques.
CO4: design the basic electronics system to acquire the different physiological parameters.
CO5: analyse the critical requirements and find the solution to design the necessary electronics.

Subject {L-T-P / C} : EE4409 : Embedded Computing Systems { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Embedded Computing System and Applications [4 hr.]
General frame work of Computing Systems, Realization of Embedded Computing Systems (ECS), Representation of ECS, Embedded Systems for Signal Processing and other applications, Design process of Embedded Computing System for Real-Time Applications.
Module 2: Interfacing for ADC and DAC [10hr.]
Finite State Machine (FSM)Representation & Design for Digital Circuits, Behavioural and Structural Description of FSM in VHDL/Verilog, Implementation of I2C and SPI communication protocols with FSM
Module 3: Embedded Architecture Design for Digital Filters [12 hr.]
Fine Grain Architecture Design: Algebraic methods for digital circuit representation and analysis, Graphic Representation of Logic Function: Decision Diagram, SDF, Spectral Transformations, Optimization of digital circuits, Arithmetic circuit, Bit and word Level Architecture Design
Coarse Grain Architecture Design: Computation Graph: Representation of DSP Algorithm as Graph, Number Representation: Multiple Word length paradigm, Measuring Throughput and Latency: Iteration and Loop Bound, Graph Transformation: Retiming, Folding & Unfolding, Pipelining and Parallel Processing, Systolic Architecture
Software-Hardware Co-Design: System-On-Chip Architecture, Soft and Hard core, Processor-Hardware Communication, Issues in SOC based realization
Digital Filter Structure: Pipelining and Parallel Systems for FIR and IIR filters, Adaptive Filter Structures, Pipelining and Parallel Systems for Adaptive filters, Scaling & Round off Noise analysis, Digital filters for low power applications
Module 4: Electronic Design Automation (EDA) Tools for Digital Filer [8 hr.]
Electronic Design Automation Tool, Hardware Description Languages and features, Embedded C, Simulation and Testing, Approximate Digital Filter Realization

Course Objective

1 .

To expose the students in order to
1. Understand the wide view of embedded computing system and its applications
2. Understand requirement analysis and design flow
3. Learn rigorously the mathematical methods for designing digital computing system
4. Learn latest Integrated Development Environment, coding in VHDL/Verilog, simulation and testing

Course Outcome

1 .

Students will be able to
CO1: Understand the scope and requirements of embedded computing systems with an abstract framework.
CO2: Analyze and formulate design problems mathematically, applying appropriate models and techniques.
CO3: Design and develop optimized DSP architectures to meet application-specific performance criteria.
CO4: Implement, evaluate, and test the performance of FIR, IIR, and Adaptive Filters.
CO5: Apply modern tools (e.g., Vivado, Vitis, MATLAB) for the design, simulation, and realization of embedded hardware systems.

Course Objective

1 .

To study the development of architecture over time (till 18th cent. CE) with focus on the Europe, East and Far-East, and Americas.
2 .

To understand the context, intentions, strategies, and relevance of different architectural movements, and styles over the time.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Ability to identify various architectural and spatial elements.
2. Ability to critically analyse different architectural styles and their elements.
3. Ability to understand the relationship between social-economic-religious-political influences on different spatial and architectural elements at building level and city level.
